claims.text: The phase transition in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by surface premelting.
Atoms at nanoparticle surfaces have reduced atomic coordination relative to atoms in the interior.
Reduced surface coordination increases local atomic vibrations and mobility and lowers local melting barriers.
Melting initiates through disorder at the particle surface and then propagates inward.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface-to-volume ratios than larger nanoparticles.
The influence of surface premelting is more pronounced in smaller particles because of their larger relative surface area.
Smaller Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will begin their phase transition at lower temperatures than larger particles.
The onset of surface disorder in smaller nanoparticles will occur tens of degrees below that in larger nanoparticles.
Structural disorder will first appear at surfaces and corners during heating.
The controlled comparison will use initially solid, crystalline nanoparticles of uniform composition that differ in size.
Particle sizes such as 5 nm, 10 nm, and 20 nm will be compared under otherwise identical heating conditions.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply under moderate heating rates and inert-environment conditions.
Extreme heating rates or compositional inhomogeneity may introduce effects outside the proposed surface-premelting mechanism.
The magnitude of melting-point depression and the phase-transition kinetics may depend on the simulation, particle shape, and local compositional fluctuations.
A lack of systematically lower premelting onset temperatures in smaller particles, or spatially uniform rather than surface-initiated melting, would falsify the hypothesis.
